evidence_quotes.quote: We study a model explaining dynamics in water coverage that accounts for ﬁnancial performances of utilities. Our dataset covers 25 Sub-Saharan countries from 1996 to 2012.

It also assesses the eﬀect of cost recovery levels on coverage rates and discusses whether the incentive structure based on cost recovery targets has a signiﬁcant eﬀect on the results of utilities in increasing those rates.
In particular, we consider the change in water coverage over the last three years measured as an absolute diﬀerence in water coverage between periods t + 3 and t (3-year diﬀerence in water coverage).
Population with access to water services (either with direct service connection or within reach of a public water point) as a percentage of the total population under utility’s nominal responsibility

While the results show that moderate levels of cost recovery are positively correlated to the improvement of water service coverage, this relationship becomes negative when high levels of cost recovery are considered.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban and peri-urban drinking-water service access provided by water utilities across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries (measured as utility water coverage via direct connection or public water points).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines regulatory, financial-policy, and institutional governance factors in urban water supply (cost-recovery targets/benchmarks under corporatization and commercialization, public fiscal expenditure, and national/regional/municipal utility organization). Under the 2026-10-13 clarification, Criterion 2 explicitly encompasses 'tariff or cost-recovery rules' and 'utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access': the paper specifically tests cost-recovery policy benchmarks and targets (operationalized via utilities' O&M cost-recovery ratio and its quadratic term to evaluate regulatory benchmark thresholds, alongside a robustness specification testing national, regional/state, and municipal utility governance structure in Model h4) and how cost-recovery rules create incentives or disincentives for extending formal water service access to unserved and low-income urban/peri-urban populations.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains original quantitative empirical analysis of an unbalanced panel dataset covering 75 water utilities (235 utility-year observations; 225 observations in models with public expenditure) across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries from 1996 to 2012, using pooled OLS, fixed-effects, random-effects, and random-effects Tobit regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports a direct service-access outcome at the utility service-area level: the three-year change in water coverage (percentage of population under the utility's nominal responsibility with access to water services via direct service connection or within reach of a public water point between periods t and t + 3).
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis and population (75 urban/peri-urban water utilities and the populations within their nominal service areas across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries, 235 utility-year observations), exposure (O&M cost-recovery ratio and squared O&M cost-recovery ratio testing cost-recovery benchmarks, plus controls including on-budget public water expenditure, non-revenue water, ODA, and national/regional/municipal utility typology), outcome (three-year percentage-point change in utility water coverage), and study design (observational unbalanced panel econometric study) are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Unbalanced longitudinal panel econometric study (pooled OLS, fixed-effects, random-effects, and random-effects Tobit regressions with lagged explanatory variables)
country: 25 Sub-Saharan African countries (Benin, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Côte d'Ivoire, Ethiopia, Gabon, Ghana, Guinea, Kenya, Lesotho, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Africa, Senegal, Sudan, Swaziland, Togo, Uganda, and Zambia)
population_and_sample: 75 urban and peri-urban water utilities across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries, observed over 1996–2012 (unbalanced panel of 235 utility-year observations; 72 utilities and 225 observations in models controlling for public expenditure)
exposure: Utility O&M cost-recovery ratio (total annual operational revenues divided by total annual operating costs, modeled linearly and quadratically to test regulatory/policy cost-recovery benchmarks), alongside on-budget public water expenditure, non-revenue water, ODA, and utility institutional level (national, regional/state, vs. municipal utilities)
outcome: Three-year change in utility water coverage (percentage-point difference between periods t + 3 and t in the share of population under the utility's nominal responsibility with access to water services via direct service connection or public water point)
rationale: This empirical panel study of 75 urban/peri-urban water utilities across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries (1996–2012) satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1–c6). It examines drinking-water service coverage (c1, c4) as a nonlinear function of utility cost-recovery ratios and regulatory/policy cost-recovery benchmarks—as well as public water spending and national/regional/municipal utility institutional structure—directly testing tariff and cost-recovery rules governing service access under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (c2), using identifiable panel econometric methods and utility-level IBNET data (c3, c5) in English (c6).
